item: Every component in the box appears in the illustrated component list, with the correct count
why: Count errors are the most common shipped defect (Obsession)

item: Every rule printed on a card, board, mat or player aid also exists in the rulebook
why: Rules that live only on a component vanish when the component does (Mage Knight, Triplock)

item: Setup is fully specified for every supported player count
why: Player-count deltas are the most re-looked-up fact in most games

item: Tie-breakers exist for every 'the most / the least / first place' rule
why: Superlatives are the classic hole-generator

item: Solo / cooperative / variant modes have their own complete setup and end conditions
why: Imperium shipped with a missing solo-bot rule

item: End-game trigger AND end-of-game sequence are both stated (does the round finish?)
why: 'Finish the round' is assumed far more often than it is written

item: Goal / win condition appears before the detailed rules
why: Readers need a purpose to attach rules to

item: No term is used before it is defined
why: The single most-cited reader irritation

item: Every forward reference cites its target section and page
why: Uncited forward references force blind page-flipping

item: Exceptions and edge cases sit beside their rule or in a clearly marked section, not inline in the core flow
why: Exceptions in the main flow make the core unlearnable

item: Each rule sits under the heading a confused player would actually reach for
why: Organisation is a retrieval problem, not only a teaching one

item: One linear read is sufficient to understand the game
why: Ryan Migalla's quality metric

item: One concept = one term, everywhere, including cards and marketing copy
why: Synonyms force readers to hunt for a difference that does not exist

item: Effects that behave identically are worded identically (templating)
why: Consistent templating lets players learn a pattern once

item: Conditions precede effects in every conditional rule
why: Reduces misplays and enables skimming

item: No sentence fails the one-breath test
why: Long sentences are the main source of parse failure

item: 'should' removed; 'exception' and 'remember' reviewed as design smells
why: Stonemaier's editorial pass

item: Repeated sets always listed in the same canonical order
why: Silent, cumulative cognitive load

item: Every example covers at least one non-obvious case
why: Obvious examples are wasted print

item: No rule appears only inside an example, caption or parenthetical
why: Paul Grogan's red flag

item: Examples make clear which details are arbitrary
why: Readers infer unintended rules from examples

item: There is a labelled setup diagram of the initial table state
why: Lets readers verify their setup visually

item: Information-dense components have an anatomy diagram
why: Converts a component into shared vocabulary

item: Table of contents present (and an index if the book exceeds ~12 pages)
why: TOC and index are different tools

item: Icon key exists in exactly one place and is easy to find
why: Icon soup without a key is a top complaint

item: Back cover carries turn flow, icon key and/or setup summary
why: The most valuable page in the book

item: A short 'commonly missed rules' list exists
why: Highest value per word available

item: Rulebook carries a version number and date
why: Enables errata and living rules

item: Body text >= 10pt (12pt preferred); test the smallest text in dim light
why: 10pt is the stated floor at Stonemaier; accessibility guidance says 12pt

item: Contrast >= 4.5:1 for body text; page still readable in greyscale
why: WCAG-derived target

item: No rules text over art, texture or dark backgrounds
why: Recurring cause of games being shelved

item: No colour-only coding anywhere; every distinction is double-coded
why: 8% of men have colour vision deficiency

item: No underlined rules text; all-caps limited to a handful of critical notes
why: Legibility

item: Short sections do not break across pages; 2-page sections are on facing pages
why: Prevents mid-rule page turns

item: Page count divisible by 4; spreads planned deliberately
why: Print reality

item: At least one full blind playtest with people who have never seen the game
why: The only reliable detector of missing rules

item: At least one blind test with non-gamers or non-native speakers
why: Experienced gamers paper over defects

item: Testers were told not to use how-to-play videos
why: Not every owner will have internet access

item: Designer did not intervene except to protect the rest of the test
why: Intervention destroys the data

item: Timed look-up test on the pre-production copy: can a specific answer be found fast?
why: Slow look-up is a structural defect

item: Rulebook read backwards, section by section, as a final QA pass
why: Prevents autopilot skimming

item: A written style guide accompanies the text to the copyeditor and proofreader
why: Cheapest possible consistency insurance

item: Editing done before layout; proofreading done after layout
why: Layout introduces its own errors

item: Instructions to the graphic designer are unmistakably not rules text
why: Bracketed notes have shipped as rules before

item: Rulebook version matches the component version being printed
why: Version drift is a classic defect source

item: Searchable PDF and a public living-rules/errata page are planned
why: Ctrl-F is the index every game already ships with
